# Data validation: does the weather data agree?

*Generated by `pipeline/validate_rain.py` from the per-field CSVs. Re-run it after a data refresh.*

Greenline uses three rainfall datasets. Two are NASA products we depend on: **NASA POWER** (~50 km, long record
back to 1984) and **GPM IMERG** (~11 km satellite rain, from 2008 in our data). We checked both against
**PRISM** (4 km, Oregon State University). PRISM is built from thousands of rain gauges and weather stations, so it's
the closest thing to "ground truth" on a grid for the U.S.

**Sample:** 201 North Texas fields. Annual: 2008–2024 (17 full years, 3,417 field-years). Monthly: 2008–2025, 42,813 field-months
(the IMERG final product we use ends in 2025-09, so 2025 is monthly only).
Each dataset is read at the field's location (the coarse pixel the field sits in).

## Annual rainfall

Average annual rain: PRISM **1024 mm**, POWER **936 mm**, IMERG **1065 mm**
(40.3 / 36.8 / 41.9 inches).

| Comparison | Correlation (all) | Median per-field correlation | Worst 10% of fields | Average difference | RMSE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NASA POWER vs PRISM | 0.92 | 0.94 | ≤ 0.90 | -89 mm (-9%) | 142 mm |
| GPM IMERG vs PRISM | 0.93 | 0.94 | ≤ 0.90 | +41 mm (+4%) | 112 mm |
| GPM IMERG vs NASA POWER | 0.95 | 0.96 | ≤ 0.93 | +130 mm (+14%) | 152 mm |

## Monthly rainfall

| Comparison | Correlation (all) | Median per-field correlation | Worst 10% of fields | Average difference | RMSE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NASA POWER vs PRISM | 0.91 | 0.92 | ≤ 0.89 | -8 mm (-9%) | 30 mm |
| GPM IMERG vs PRISM | 0.91 | 0.91 | ≤ 0.89 | +3 mm (+3%) | 29 mm |
| GPM IMERG vs NASA POWER | 0.95 | 0.95 | ≤ 0.93 | +11 mm (+14%) | 22 mm |

## Heavy-rain days (≥ 25 mm, about 1 inch, in a day)

| | PRISM | IMERG |
|---|---|---|
| Average days per year | 12.4 | 12.7 |

IMERG counts **+2%** heavy-rain days compared with PRISM. Field-year correlation: 0.71. Year-to-year
correlation of the regional average: 0.90. Caveat: PRISM "days" run 12:00–12:00 UTC (≈ 7 am–7 am local)
and IMERG days run midnight–midnight UTC, so one storm can be split differently.

## Frost-free season (last spring frost to first fall frost, Tmin ≤ 0 °C)

PRISM vs POWER, 1984–2025, 8,324 field-years: correlation 0.68. On average, POWER's season is
**+3 days** longer than PRISM's (median +0). PRISM's average season is 254 days and POWER's is 257.
POWER found no fall frost at all in 2 year(s), so the frost-free season can't be computed for those years.

## What this means

- **Year-to-year rain is trustworthy.** Both NASA datasets track the gauge-based reference closely for annual
  totals (correlation 0.92 for POWER, 0.93 for IMERG). Driest year (2008–2024, regional average): PRISM 2011,
  POWER 2011, IMERG 2014 (2011 ranks #1, #1, #2 driest). Wettest year: PRISM 2015, POWER 2015, IMERG 2015.
- **Totals are slightly off.** Compared with PRISM, POWER reads -9% and IMERG +4% on annual rain. POWER runs dry, so
  rain amounts shown from POWER should be read as approximate (about ±10%).
- **Single months at single fields are noisier.** A typical month is off by about 29 mm, and POWER's 50 km cells blur
  local thunderstorms. That's one reason the weather-stress model (model 2) is weak and is shown only as a low-confidence signal.
- **Heavy-rain days:** IMERG and PRISM agree on the average count (12.7 vs 12.4 days a year), so the earlier worry that IMERG overcounts
  storm days (MODELS.md, caveat 11, which compared it with POWER) is not supported. For a single field in a single year they agree less well (r = 0.71).
- **Not fully independent.** IMERG's monthly product is adjusted with gauge data (GPCC), and POWER's rain is
  bias-corrected with gauge analyses. Good agreement is consistency evidence, not proof from a separate source.
  Next step: CoCoRaHS volunteer gauges (see `datasets.md`, Future additions).
